steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on spatio-temporal (ST) prediction that argues existing graph-based models mix together the effects of many latent factors. Introduce a multi-factor ST prediction task and our graph decomposition learning framework, list the contributions, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- ST data and applications of ST prediction
- Existing work: temporal and spatial perspectives
- Limitation: holistic scheme ignores multiple latent factors
- Our approach: multi-factor ST prediction task, decomposed prediction strategy, STGDL framework, experiments
- Contributions
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- ST data and applications
  - GPS-enabled mobile devices and sensors -> huge volume of ST data: urban transportation, meteorology, public health
  - ST prediction techniques (cite) support applications from individual smart mobility (cite) to public safety management (cite)
  - e.g. ST traffic prediction: forecast future traffic from past observations; bike-sharing for green commuting (cite), congestion management for traffic efficiency (cite)
- Existing work
  - temporal: evolution over time, closeness, periodicity, trend (cite); RNNs e.g. LSTM (cite), temporal convolutional networks (cite), attention (cite)
  - spatial: relations of regions/sensors (cite); all mixed into one global graph; GNNs for holistic spatial dependency (cite), attention for aggregation over whole graph (cite)
- Limitation
  - holistic scheme: whole original graph
  - ignore nuances among partial ST data affected by different latent factors; each factor affects only relevant nodes and relations
  - traffic: follows human mobility law in socioeconomic interactions (cite); driven by commuting, entertainment, business, etc.; each factor -> different regions, different flows (cite)
  - entangled relations -> need to decouple; unexplored
  - result: mixture of entangled factors, hurts interpretability and understanding of ST evolution
- Our approach
  - multi-factor ST prediction task: forecast each latent factor separately, integrate for final prediction
  - STGDL (Spatio-Temporal Graph Decomposition Learning)
  - decomposed prediction strategy: divide-and-conquer, original graph -> subgraphs, learn ST data on each, integrate
  - theoretically guaranteed smaller prediction error than predicting on original graph
  - STGDL: automatic graph decomposition (matrix masking + two regularization terms: graph completeness, subgraph independence) and decomposed learning networks (forward and backward residual connections, stack of ST blocks, one block per factor's subgraph)
  - four public ST benchmarks: two grid graph-based, two network graph-based; improves graph-based ST models by 9.41% on average
- Contributions (four)
  - first to handle multi-factor issue; new task, theoretically guaranteed portable framework
  - decomposed prediction strategy; proof it reduces errors
  - portable STGDL framework; disentangled ST embedding per factor
  - experiments on four real-world datasets; case study on interpretability
- Organization: Sec. II concepts and problem; Sec. III theoretical solution; Sec. IV framework; Sec. V evaluation; Sec. VI related work; Sec. VII conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Because GPS-enabled mobile devices and sensors are used everywhere, a huge volume of spatio-temporal (ST) data is coming from many domains, e.g., urban transportation, meteorology, and public health. With ST prediction techniques, the ST data can support more and more applications, from individual smart mobility to public safety management. For example, ST traffic prediction, which tries to accurately forecast future traffic conditions from past traffic observations, can promote environmentally friendly commuting with bike-sharing initiatives, and it can improve traffic efficiency with congestion management.

Existing studies on ST data usually look at it from a temporal and a spatial perspective. The temporal perspective is about how the data evolves over time, which covers patterns of closeness, periodicity, and trend. Researchers use recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTM), temporal convolutional networks, or attention mechanism to encode the temporal features of traffic series. The spatial perspective, on the other hand, is mainly about the relations between different spatial regions or sensors in the study area. All of these relations are mixed together into a global graph structure. Most efforts use graph neural networks to model spatial dependency holistically, or attention mechanism to aggregate spatial information across the whole graph.

These methods have had notable successes, but they generally use a holistic scheme, i.e., they characterize ST data on the original graph structure as a whole. They ignore the nuances among parts of the ST data that are affected by different latent factors. Each factor may only affect the relevant graph nodes and relations and not the whole graph. If we take traffic ST data as an example, the formation of traffic flow usually follows the human mobility law in real-world socioeconomic interactions. It is driven by many complex latent factors, like commuting, entertainment, business, etc. Each of them focuses on different urban regions and forms different traffic flows. Because the relations among multiple latent factors are complex and entangled, there is an urgent need to decouple these factors in ST data prediction. The existing works have not explored this. So the predicted ST data contains a mixture of entangled factors, and this inevitably harms interpretability and makes it hard to fully understand how the ST data evolves.

- our approach: multi-factor ST prediction task (forecast each latent factor separately, integrate partial results)
  - STGDL: Spatio-Temporal Graph Decomposition Learning
  - decomposed prediction strategy: divide-and-conquer, original graph -> subgraphs, learn on each, integrate; theoretically smaller error than original graph
  - automatic graph decomposition: matrix masking, two regularizers (graph completeness, subgraph independence)
  - decomposed learning networks: forward and backward residual connections, stack of ST blocks, one block per factor
  - four public benchmarks (two grid graph-based, two network graph-based); +9.41% on average for graph-based ST models
- contributions: first on multi-factor issue + new task; decomposed prediction strategy with proof; portable STGDL, disentangled embedding per factor; experiments on four datasets + interpretability case study
- organization: Sec. II concepts/problem; Sec. III theory; Sec. IV framework; Sec. V evaluation; Sec. VI related work; Sec. VII conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Because GPS-enabled mobile devices and sensors are used everywhere, a huge volume of spatio-temporal (ST) data is coming from many domains, e.g., urban transportation, meteorology, and public health. With ST prediction techniques, the ST data can support more and more applications, from individual smart mobility to public safety management. For example, ST traffic prediction, which tries to accurately forecast future traffic conditions from past traffic observations, can promote environmentally friendly commuting with bike-sharing initiatives, and it can improve traffic efficiency with congestion management.

Existing studies on ST data usually look at it from a temporal and a spatial perspective. The temporal perspective is about how the data evolves over time, which covers patterns of closeness, periodicity, and trend. Researchers use recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTM), temporal convolutional networks, or attention mechanism to encode the temporal features of traffic series. The spatial perspective, on the other hand, is mainly about the relations between different spatial regions or sensors in the study area. All of these relations are mixed together into a global graph structure. Most efforts use graph neural networks to model spatial dependency holistically, or attention mechanism to aggregate spatial information across the whole graph.

These methods have had notable successes, but they generally use a holistic scheme, i.e., they characterize ST data on the original graph structure as a whole. They ignore the nuances among parts of the ST data that are affected by different latent factors. Each factor may only affect the relevant graph nodes and relations and not the whole graph. If we take traffic ST data as an example, the formation of traffic flow usually follows the human mobility law in real-world socioeconomic interactions. It is driven by many complex latent factors, like commuting, entertainment, business, etc. Each of them focuses on different urban regions and forms different traffic flows. Because the relations among multiple latent factors are complex and entangled, there is an urgent need to decouple these factors in ST data prediction. The existing works have not explored this. So the predicted ST data contains a mixture of entangled factors, and this inevitably harms interpretability and makes it hard to fully understand how the ST data evolves.

In this paper we propose a multi-factor spatio-temporal prediction task to deal with the multi-factor issue. The task is to forecast the ST data evolution of multiple latent factors separately and then integrate all the partial results into the final ST prediction. We design a new Spatio-Temporal Graph Decomposition Learning framework (STGDL) that can do multi-factor spatio-temporal prediction. Specifically, we first propose a theoretical solution called the decomposed prediction strategy. It follows the divide-and-conquer paradigm: the strategy decomposes the original graph structure, which mixes multiple factors, into several subgraphs. Then we can learn the relevant ST data on each subgraph separately and integrate them to get an overall traffic prediction. More importantly, we show that the proposed strategy is theoretically guaranteed to have a smaller prediction error than predicting directly on the original graph. Next, we instantiate the strategy as a framework called STGDL, and its key components are automatic graph decomposition and decomposed learning networks. The first component is implemented by matrix masking with two regularization terms that preserve the principles of graph completeness and subgraph independence. The second component is based on forward and backward residual connections and a stack of ST blocks. Each block is responsible for learning ST data on the subgraph relevant to a certain factor. We do extensive experiments on four public ST benchmarks, two grid graph-based datasets and two network graph-based datasets. The results show that our STGDL can improve the performance of a wide range of graph-based ST models by 9.41% on average. Our contributions are four-fold:

- As far as we know, this research is the first to deal with the multi-factor issue for ST prediction. So we introduce a multi-factor ST prediction task and solve it with a portable framework that is theoretically guaranteed.

- We propose a decomposed prediction strategy that achieves multi-factor ST prediction through graph decomposition in a divide-and-conquer way. We prove that the strategy can reduce ST prediction errors.

- We design a portable STGDL framework that instantiates the proposed strategy with automatic graph decomposition and decomposed learning networks. The framework can learn a disentangled ST embedding for each latent factor.

- Extensive experiments on four real-world ST datasets show the performance gain of the STGDL plugin on various graph-based ST models. Also, a case study confirms that the learned patterns can give interpretability for deep models and their predictions.

The rest of the paper is organized like this: Sec. II introduces the basic concepts and the problem of multi-factor ST prediction. Sec. III proposes a theoretical solution for the problem, and Sec. IV instantiates it as an ST graph decomposition learning framework. Sec. V evaluates the proposed framework on four public datasets with various baselines. The related work is in Sec. VI and the conclusion is in Sec. VII.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the ubiquitous use of GPS-enabled mobile devices and sensors, a huge volume of spatio-temporal (ST) data is emerging from a variety of domains, e.g., urban transportation, meteorology, and public health. Through ST prediction techniques [1,2,3,4], ST data can support a growing number of applications ranging from individual smart mobility [5] to public safety management [6]. For example, ST traffic prediction, which aims to accurately forecast future traffic conditions from past traffic observations, can promote environmentally friendly commuting through bike-sharing initiatives [7,8], and enhance traffic efficiency through congestion management [9,10].

Existing studies on ST data usually take a temporal and a spatial perspective. The temporal perspective describes the evolution trends of the data over time, covering patterns of closeness, periodicity, and trend [11,12]. Researchers apply recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTM) [13,14], temporal convolutional networks [15,16], or attention mechanisms [17] to encode the temporal features of traffic series. The spatial perspective, on the other hand, mainly describes the relations of different spatial regions or sensors in the study area [18,19]. All the relations are mixed together to form a global graph structure. Main efforts deploy graph neural networks for holistic spatial dependency modeling [20,4,21], or attention mechanisms for spatial information aggregation across the whole graph [3,16].

Despite their notable successes, existing methods generally adopt a holistic scheme, i.e., they characterize ST data on the original graph structure as a whole. They ignore the nuances among partial ST data affected by different latent factors, although each factor may only affect relevant graph nodes and relations rather than the whole. Taking traffic ST data as an example, the formation of traffic flow typically follows the human mobility law in real-world socioeconomic interactions [22]. It is driven by many complex latent factors, such as commuting, entertainment, business, etc., each of which focuses on different urban regions and forms different traffic flows [23,24,25,26]. The complex and entangled relations among multiple latent factors create an urgent need to decouple these factors in ST data prediction, which remains unexplored by existing works. As a result, the predicted ST data contains a mixture of entangled factors, inevitably harming interpretability and making it difficult to thoroughly understand the evolution of ST data.

In this paper, we propose a multi-factor spatio-temporal prediction task to tackle the multi-factor issue. The task aims to forecast the ST data evolution of multiple latent factors separately and then integrate all partial results for the final ST prediction. We design a novel Spatio-Temporal Graph Decomposition Learning framework (STGDL) capable of multi-factor spatio-temporal prediction. Specifically, we first propose a theoretical solution called the decomposed prediction strategy. Following the divide-and-conquer paradigm, the strategy decomposes the original graph structure that mixes multiple factors into several subgraphs. We can then learn relevant ST data on each subgraph separately and integrate them to produce an overall traffic prediction. More importantly, we show that the proposed strategy is theoretically guaranteed to have a smaller prediction error than predicting directly on the original graph. Next, we instantiate the strategy as a framework called STGDL, whose key components are automatic graph decomposition and decomposed learning networks. The former is implemented by matrix masking with two regularization terms that preserve the principles of graph completeness and subgraph independence. The latter is based on forward and backward residual connections and a stack of ST blocks, each of which is responsible for learning ST data on the subgraph relevant to a certain factor. We conduct extensive experiments on four public ST benchmarks, including two grid graph-based datasets and two network graph-based datasets. The results show that STGDL can enhance the performance of a wide range of graph-based ST models by an average of 9.41%. Our contributions are four-fold:

- To our knowledge, this research is the first to deal with the multi-factor issue for ST prediction. We introduce a multi-factor ST prediction task and solve it with a theoretically guaranteed portable framework.

- We propose a decomposed prediction strategy that achieves multi-factor ST prediction via graph decomposition in a divide-and-conquer fashion, and we prove that the strategy can reduce ST prediction errors.

- We design a portable STGDL framework that instantiates the proposed strategy through automatic graph decomposition and decomposed learning networks. The framework can learn a disentangled ST embedding for each latent factor.

- Extensive experiments on four real-world ST datasets show the performance gain achieved by the STGDL plugin on various graph-based ST models. Moreover, a case study confirms that the learned patterns can provide interpretability for deep models and their predictions.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Sec. II introduces the basic concepts and the problem of multi-factor ST prediction. Sec. III proposes a theoretical solution for this problem, and Sec. IV instantiates it as an ST graph decomposition learning framework. Sec. V evaluates the proposed framework on four public datasets with various baselines. The related work and conclusion are presented in Sec. VI and VII, respectively.

References:

[2] P. Xie, M. Ma, T. Li, S. Ji, S. Du, Z. Yu, and J. Zhang, “Spatio-temporal dynamic graph relation learning for urban metro flow prediction,” IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering , vol. 35, no. 10, pp. 9973–9984, 2023.

[4] S. Guo, Y. Lin, H. Wan, X. Li, and G. Cong, “Learning dynamics and heterogeneity of spatial-temporal graph data for traffic forecasting,” IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering , vol. 34, no. 11, pp. 5415–5428, 2021.
